sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Feet Elevated Hip Thrust is a glute-focused hip extension exercise where the feet are raised on a platform such as bumper plates or a low box.

Elevating the feet increases hamstring involvement and changes the loading angle on the glutes, providing a deeper stretch and stronger contraction compared to standard hip thrusts.

This variation is excellent for developing the posterior chain without heavy external loading, making it suitable for all training levels.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Strong emphasis on gluteus maximus and hamstrings
- Increased range of motion compared to flat-footed hip thrusts
- Builds glute strength and power for athletic performance
- Improves hip extension mechanics
- Bodyweight-friendly variation - no heavy loading required
- Enhances mind-muscle connection with the glutes
- Reduced lower back stress compared to conventional deadlifts
- Supports better posture and pelvic alignment
- Excellent accessory for squats and deadlifts

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Gluteus Maximus, Hamstrings

Secondary: Gluteus Medius, Adductors, Core, Erector Spinae, Quadriceps

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Position a bench or box behind you for upper back support.
2. Place bumper plates (or a low platform) where your feet will rest.
3. Sit on the ground with your upper back against the edge of the bench.
4. Place your feet flat on the bumper plates, hip-width apart.
5. Arms can rest on the bench or extend along your sides for stability.
6. Tuck your chin slightly to maintain a neutral head position.
7. Engage your core and set your pelvis in a neutral position.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Take a deep breath and brace your core.
2. Drive through your heels on the elevated platform.
3. Lift your hips toward the ceiling by squeezing your glutes.
4. Continue until your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees.
5. Pause at the top and maximally contract your glutes.
6. Avoid hyperextending the lower back at the top.
7. Lower your hips back down with control.
8. Stop just before your glutes touch the floor to maintain tension.
9. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Hyperextending the lower back at the top
- Pushing through the toes instead of the heels
- Tucking the chin too aggressively or looking up
- Not achieving full hip extension at the top
- Letting the knees cave inward
- Using momentum instead of glute drive
- Feet positioned too far from the body
- Upper back slipping off the bench
- Resting on the floor between reps (losing tension)

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Flat Bench or Low Box (for upper back support)
- Bumper Plates or Low Platform (for foot elevation)
- Padded Mat (optional for comfort)
- Optional: Glute Band (for added resistance)
- Optional: Dumbbell or Barbell (for added load)
- Recommended: Non-slip surface for stability

sections.heading: Foot Elevation Setup
sections.content:
1. Use stable bumper plates or a low box (4-8 inches high).
2. Ensure the platform is wide enough for full foot contact.
3. Position feet so knees are bent at approximately 90 degrees at the top.
4. Feet should be hip-width apart with toes forward or slightly out.
5. Avoid unstable surfaces that can tip or shift.
6. Ensure the platform has a non-slip surface.
7. Test stability with bodyweight before adding load.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Upper Back: Rested on bench edge at the bra-line / shoulder blades.
2. Stance: Feet on platform, hip-width apart.
3. Knees: Bent approximately 90 degrees at the top position.
4. Hips: Aligned with shoulders and knees at lockout.
5. Spine: Neutral - avoid hyperextension.
6. Core: Braced throughout the entire movement.
7. Chin: Slightly tucked, head neutral.
8. Arms: Resting on bench or along sides for balance.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Barbell Hip Thrust: Heavy loaded variation with barbell
- Dumbbell Hip Thrust: Dumbbell load across the hips
- Glute Bridge: Floor-based variation without bench
- Single Leg Hip Thrust: Unilateral version for balance and stability
- Kas Glute Bridge: Limited range of motion for constant glute tension
- B-Stance Hip Thrust: Staggered foot position for quasi-unilateral loading

sections.heading: Hip Thrust Variations
sections.content:
Feet Elevated Hip Thrust: Feet on platform for increased range
Barbell Hip Thrust: Loaded variation for strength
Dumbbell Hip Thrust: Dumbbell on hips for moderate load
Single Leg Hip Thrust: Unilateral challenge
B-Stance Hip Thrust: Staggered stance with partial unilateral load
Paused Hip Thrust: Pause at top for increased time under tension
Banded Hip Thrust: Resistance band for constant glute tension
Tempo Hip Thrust: Slow eccentric for hypertrophy

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Pain: Reduce range of motion, focus on glute squeeze without hyperextending
Knee Pain: Ensure proper foot placement, reduce load
Hip Pinching: Adjust foot position wider or closer to body
Neck Strain: Support head with small towel, avoid looking up
No Bench: Perform on floor as standard glute bridge
No Bumper Plates: Use stacked books, aerobic step, or any stable elevated surface
Beginner Stage: Master the standard hip thrust before adding foot elevation
